NFL.com’s Kevin Patra also flagged depth concerns, noting that a few injuries to key players could create havoc. That makes Denver’s margin for error thin even with an elite-looking starting 22. [4]

- **Jonah Elliss** — Denver is moving Elliss from a pure outside linebacker role to at least some inside-linebacker snaps this season. Nik Bonitto said Elliss was already lining up inside on third downs and is one of the team’s best coverage players. That suggests a broader package role and gives Denver another flexible piece in sub-defense, even if it is not a full-time switch. [7]

- **Mike McGlinchey** — Denver’s long-term plan at right tackle is not straightforward, with McGlinchey carrying two more non-guaranteed years on his deal and a sizable 2026/2027 cap charge. The Broncos also have a 2028 void year hanging over the contract, so there is real roster-building value in deciding whether to keep, restructure, or move on. For fantasy, it matters indirectly through Bo Nix’s protection and the offense’s stability. [8]

KC.summary: - **Vincent Anthony Jr.** — The undrafted Duke edge rusher is headed to Chiefs training camp after finishing college with 15 sacks, 8 batted passes and a forced fumble. Kansas City’s bottom-of-the-depth-chart defensive end spots are open enough that he has a real shot to earn rotation snaps, especially with second-round pick R Mason Thomas the only drafted DE. His “Vyper” edge style gives the Chiefs another developmental pass-rush option if he translates it quickly. [6]

MIN.summary:
- **Jennings** — Minnesota’s cap planning assumes his signing will be reflected soon, and the expected hit is around $4 million with void years possible. That helps frame how much room the Vikings have for rookies and any additional veteran additions. [2]

- **O’Neill** — The Vikings are still hoping to work out an extension that could lower his cap hit by roughly $5–8 million. If that happens, it would create more flexibility for other moves while keeping a key blocker’s contract manageable. [2]

- **Rob Brzinski / the Vikings’ front office** — The GM search appears to be clouded by concerns that top candidates may not get real authority, with Chad Alexander cited as a possible interviewer who could decline. That matters because the org chart may be shifting toward a president of football ops model, which could affect who actually controls roster-building. [5]

- **Minnesota Vikings / NFL Draft** — The expectation is that Minneapolis will be awarded the 2028 NFL Draft at this week’s league meetings, though it is not officially done yet. That would be a major event for the franchise and the city, bringing another big-stage league showcase to U.S. Bank Stadium. [7]

CLE.summary:
- **Deshaun Watson** — Watson is reportedly favored to start Cleveland’s Week 1 opener over Shedeur Sanders in a four-man QB competition that also includes Dillon Gabriel and rookie Taylen Green. That keeps the Browns’ most fantasy-relevant job unsettled, but it also gives Watson the clearest path to opening-day snaps if the competition plays out as expected. [5, 8]

- **Joe Royer** — The Browns used a fifth-round pick on Royer, a 6-foot-0, 255-pound tight end from Cincinnati who posted 79 catches for 937 yards and seven touchdowns in his final two college seasons. He’s being framed as a possible complement to Harold Fannin Jr., which matters because Cleveland may lean on multiple-TE usage to support the passing game. [7]

- **Todd Monken** — Cleveland’s offseason has been credited for veteran offensive-line additions and a broader roster reset under first-year head coach Monken. The biggest unfinished item remains the quarterback situation, but the work up front suggests the Browns want to stabilize the offense around whoever wins the job. [8]

- **Browns schedule** — Cleveland’s 2026 slate is being viewed as favorable enough to put the team in range for a 6-4 or 7-3 record by the bye week. The appeal comes from a last-place schedule with several opponents coming off down seasons, which could make the Browns a sneaky early-season DFS/fantasy streamer spot depending on the QB outcome. [3]

LAC.summary:
- **Chargers schedule** — Los Angeles got only three primetime games despite back-to-back 11-win, playoff seasons, while Kansas City was handed six. The slate is also being framed as difficult early and through some brutal stretches, so the team may have to earn attention the hard way. [4, 7]

- **Mike McDaniel** — The new offensive coordinator is setting a high bar for the Chargers’ wide receiver room, pushing for career-best production across the board. That matters because the offense did not produce a 1,000-yard receiver or rusher in 2025, so McDaniel’s scheme fit and target distribution could reshape fantasy value. [6]

- **Jacob Spomer** — The Chargers added the Fresno State center as an undrafted free agent and are giving him a look as an interior offensive line prospect after he spent his first three college seasons at left tackle. His path is interesting because he has tackle history, but the team is exploring him at center, which could make him a depth-chart sleeper if he sticks. [5]

IND.summary:
- **Anthony Richardson Sr.** — He is expected to remain with the Colts and says he’s grateful for another chance to work and potentially get on the field in 2026. The item says he’s in a backup competition with Riley Leonard behind Daniel Jones, so Richardson’s immediate value is roster depth, but the QB room still has a live competition for the No. 2 job. [8]

- **Spencer Shrader / Blake Grupe** — The Colts have a real kicker battle between Shrader and Grupe, with both viewed as viable answers. Shrader’s case is cleaner accuracy: he went 13-for-14 on field goals and 14-for-14 on extra points before his knee injury, while Grupe’s appeal is the bigger leg and a strong late-season stretch. This matters because the job could come down to trust vs. range, and neither side appears to have a decisive edge yet. [4]

- **Chris Hewitt** — The Colts’ defensive passing game coordinator and secondary coach is being positioned as a rising coach who is expected to keep climbing the ladder. That does not change a fantasy chart directly, but it reinforces continuity on Lou Anarumo’s staff and suggests Hewitt is building head-coach credibility internally. [7]

- **Shane Steichen** — Indianapolis’ 2026 slate includes a set of road matchups being flagged as the toughest tests, with Kansas City singled out as a major challenge. The schedule piece also notes the Colts open with Baltimore before that Week 2 trip to Kansas City, so the early-season road run could shape the team’s start. [5]

CIN.summary:
- **Connor Lew** — Cincinnati used the 128th pick on the Auburn center, who started all three seasons there and earned the job as a true freshman. The profile points to a smart, athletic interior fit for the Bengals’ O-line room, with his run-game angles and second-level ability standing out. His ACL tear in his junior season is part of the context, so the key watch is how he recovers and whether he can push for future center snaps. [3]

- **Colbie Young** — The rookie wideout said he sees a “blessing” in landing behind Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, because it should create more one-on-one chances. He’s already talking up trust, learning the playbook, and contributing on special teams, which signals an early path to a role beyond just camp depth. For fantasy, he’s a name to monitor in a WR3/WR4 competition if he can translate his size and opportunity into usage. [8]

- **Demetrius Knight Jr. and Barrett Carter** — Cincinnati did not overhaul the linebacker room, instead leaning on the young duo after adding help elsewhere on defense. The item notes both struggled as rookies: Carter was often fooled by backfield action, while Knight got better late but still had issues in space and at bad angles. That makes linebacker the clearest weakness on the depth chart and a unit to watch for any in-season emergence. [6]

CAR.summary:
- **Bryce Young** — The Panthers’ support around Young is still being framed as inadequate: the offense has improved since his rookie year, but the receiving help still “didn’t add much beyond” Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker, and he’s still forced into a lot of tight-window throws. The supporting context is that even in 2025 he completed 79% of his under-pressure throws to open receivers, underscoring how much he’s having to do on his own. That keeps the passing-game ceiling tied to whether Carolina can add more dependable targets. [6]

- **Panthers** — Carolina is being urged to add a free agent, but the emphasis in this item is that the team probably should not chase the splashy offensive names like Deebo Samuel, Jonnu Smith, Tyreek Hill, Darren Waller, or DeAndre Hopkins. The more immediate roster need is described as linebacker help, which suggests the front office may be looking for a lower-cost, short-term upgrade rather than another headline skill-player move. - **Darren Waller** — said Mike McDaniel’s end-of-tenure plan was to “give the keys” to Quinn Ewers and bring in competition around him, with other staff changes also apparently on the table. That suggests Miami was already preparing for a quarterback reset before the coaching change hit. It also makes Tua Tagovailoa’s future look even more distant than the coaching transition alone would suggest. [3, 6]

- **Dolphins** — are entering the Jon-Eric Sullivan/Jeff Hafley era, and the schedule note points to several early storylines: the opener against the Raiders, Jeff Hafley’s return to Lambeau Field, and Mike McDaniel’s return to Hard Rock Stadium. Those games matter because they’ll be the first real look at how Miami’s new direction holds up against league-wide attention spots. [5]

- **Malik Willis** — is being discussed as the possible new “face of the franchise” for Miami after Tua Tagovailoa moved on, with De’Von Achane also mentioned as an alternative in the team discussion. The item doesn’t specify any competition details, but it does show the Dolphins’ identity at quarterback is still in flux. [7]
